issues.legal_issue: A religious-endowment scheme cannot be imposed by an executive officer without judicial oversight where it unreasonably restricts the institution’s property rights.
material_facts: The Commissioner, an administrative officer, could frame a scheme for a religious institution.

After amendment, the Commissioner’s scheme order was made final and conclusive, with no effective civil-court review, although a related provision still referred to a court’s power to set aside or modify a scheme.
The scheme could affect the superior’s control of the institution, an office blended with property rights.
issues.conclusion: The provisions authorizing the Commissioner to frame the scheme were invalid as unreasonable restrictions on fundamental rights.
issues.legal_principle: Under Articles 19(1)(f), 25 and 26, control of religious endowments must not impose an unreasonable restriction on property or protected religious rights. An executive officer’s scheme-making power without intervention of a judicial tribunal is an unreasonable restriction. The Court applied the principles discussed in The Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments, Madras v. Sri Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar, Civil Appeal No. 38 of 1953, and considered the scheme provisions and the inconsistent provision for court review.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_religious_en: A party challenges the constitutionality of rules governing the administration of a religious endowment.
predicates.scheme_set_by_administrative_officer: An administrative officer, rather than a court, sets the management scheme for the institution.
predicates.scheme_order_lacks_effective_court_revie: The scheme order cannot effectively be challenged or reviewed by a court.
predicates.scheme_affects_property_or_management_ri: The scheme affects rights in endowed property or the institution’s management.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns an administrative scheme that affects property or management rights and lacks effective court review, the scheme provisions are invalid.

issues.legal_issue: A restriction allowing an administrator to direct how an institution’s surplus income may be used is invalid when it curtails the superior’s discretion to spend that income for the institution’s benefit.
material_facts: The law allowed a Math’s superior wide powers over surplus income, subject to a restriction against personal spending unconnected with the dignity of the office.
The purposes permitted by the section were conducive to the institution’s benefit.
The proviso allowed the Commissioner to issue directions that further restricted the superior’s discretion over that spending.
issues.conclusion: The proviso restricting the superior’s discretion over the use of surplus income was invalid.
issues.legal_principle: Articles 19(1)(f), 25 and 26 protect against unreasonable interference with property and religious rights. Although regulation may ensure proper administration, further executive restrictions on the use of surplus income for purposes beneficial to the institution were not justified. The Court applied the principles discussed in The Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments, Madras v. Sri Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar, Civil Appeal No. 38 of 1953.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_religious_en: A party challenges the constitutionality of rules governing the administration of a religious endowment.
predicates.superior_has_discretion_over_surplus_for: The institution’s superior may use surplus income for purposes benefiting the institution, subject to limits against personal use unrelated to the office.
predicates.administrator_can_further_restrict_that_: An administrator may issue directions that further limit the superior’s discretion over that income.

issues.definition: If a constitutional challenge concerns an administrator’s power to further restrict a superior’s use of surplus income for institutional benefit, the restriction is invalid.

issues.legal_issue: An annual contribution earmarked for the administration of religious institutions is a fee rather than a tax and may be imposed by the legislature with authority over that subject.
material_facts: Institutions above the stated income threshold had to make an annual contribution toward the Commissioner’s office and staff.
The contributions formed part of a special fund used to administer the endowment law and were not merged into general public revenue.
The fund was specifically set apart for the services involved in administering the institutions.
issues.conclusion: The contribution was a fee, not a tax, and the legislature was competent to enact it.
issues.legal_principle: A fee is imposed in consideration of services or work for the benefit of those from whom it is demanded, and its proceeds must be specifically appropriated for that purpose rather than merged into general revenue. The distinction between fees and taxes and the application of those principles followed The Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments, Madras v. Sri Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar, Civil Appeal No. 38 of 1953.

predicates.challenge_to_legislative_competence_over: A party challenges the legislature’s competence to impose an annual levy on institutions.
predicates.levy_funds_administration_services_for_c: The levy is collected to fund administration services connected with the contributing institutions.
predicates.proceeds_are_set_apart_for_those_service: The proceeds are specifically appropriated to those services rather than merged into general public revenue.

issues.definition: When an annual levy funds administration services for contributing institutions and its proceeds are set apart for those services, it is a fee within legislative competence.

issues.legal_issue: A contribution used for the secular administration of religious institutions does not constitute an appropriation for promoting or maintaining a religion.
material_facts: The contribution funded the Commissioner and the administrative machinery for religious trusts and institutions.
The proceeds were applied to the proper administration of those institutions, not to foster or preserve a religion or denomination.
issues.conclusion: The contribution did not violate Article 27.
issues.legal_principle: Article 27 prohibits the specific appropriation of tax proceeds to pay expenses for the promotion or maintenance of a particular religion or religious denomination. A contribution directed to the secular administration of religious institutions, without favoring a religion or denomination, does not fall within that prohibition.

predicates.challenge_to_a_religious_institution_con: A party challenges a contribution imposed on religious institutions.
predicates.proceeds_fund_secular_administration: The proceeds fund the secular administration of religious trusts and institutions.
predicates.proceeds_do_not_promote_or_maintain_a_re: The proceeds are not used to foster or preserve a religion or religious denomination.

issues.definition: If a challenged contribution funds secular administration and does not promote or maintain a religion, it does not violate the religious-funding restriction.

issues.legal_issue: Purpose-limited supervisory powers, ordinary trustee duties, lawful administrative orders, and access to civil-court review do not make the challenged administrative provisions invalid.
material_facts: The Commissioner’s supervisory powers were directed to proper maintenance of institutions and administration of endowments.
The trustee’s duties reflected the care expected of an ordinarily prudent person managing trust property.
A trustee was required to obey only lawful orders made within the officer’s authority.
A person aggrieved by an order applying surplus funds under the relevant provision could bring a civil suit to have the order modified or set aside.
issues.conclusion: The Court found no sufficient ground to invalidate the other challenged administrative provisions on these bases.
issues.legal_principle: A supervisory power confined to ensuring proper administration is not arbitrary merely because it is broad; ordinary fiduciary duties and compliance with lawful orders do not themselves interfere with fundamental rights. Availability of civil-court review also answers a complaint about an administrative order. The Court applied the principles discussed in The Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments, Madras v. Sri Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar, Civil Appeal No. 38 of 1953.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_administration_provisions and (supervisory_power_is_confined_to_proper_management or trustee_duty_is_ordinary_and_prudent or order_must_be_lawful_and_within_authority or civil_court_review_is_available)

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_administrati: A party challenges rules governing supervision or administration of a religious institution.
predicates.supervisory_power_is_confined_to_proper_: The administrator’s supervisory power is directed to proper maintenance and management of the institution and its endowment.
predicates.trustee_duty_is_ordinary_and_prudent: The trustee is required to exercise the care expected of an ordinarily prudent person managing trust property.
predicates.order_must_be_lawful_and_within_authorit: The trustee must obey only an order that is lawful and within the administrator’s authority.
predicates.civil_court_review_is_available: A person affected by the administrative order may seek civil-court review of it.

issues.definition: When a challenged administrative provision has at least one of the stated safeguards or ordinary fiduciary features, it remains valid.
